text: Least privilege asked if one account has too much access. Segregation of duties asks a different question: can one person, alone, complete an entire sensitive process end to end?

The classic case is accounts payable. Who creates a vendor record. Who approves it. Who issues payment. If the same person does all three, there's no independent check — which is exactly how a lot of payment fraud actually happens. Split it across three people, and fraud now requires collusion.

This maps directly onto the four access-governance roles from Lesson 12. If the same person requests their own access and approves it, there's no independent check on that grant — the identical flaw, just applied to access instead of money.

An SoD program names toxic combinations — permission pairs that should never sit with one person. Can grant access, plus can approve your own request. Can write the audit log, plus no independent review of it. A conflict matrix lists these pairs so reviews can catch them.
Next up: access reviews and certification — the recurring process that catches SoD violations and permission creep after they've already accumulated.
